newsitem.title: CANADA: MacMillan says paper merger would make sense.
newsitem.headline: MacMillan says paper merger would make sense.

text.p: Amid market speculation that it may divest its paper division, MacMillan Bloedel Ltd said on Wednesday that merging the operation with another paper maker would make sense but that nothing was planned.
Chief Executive Robert Findlay told reporters after the annual meeting that the paper division "probably should be merged" as Abitibi-Price Inc did with Stone Consolidated Corp.
The logical partner would be Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd, but a deal was unlikely despite many years of talks between the two companies, he said.
Findlay said MacMillan had no other potential partners in mind, although it was "always having discussions."

"All I would say about the paper business is that it is as good as most in Canada. But it probably should be merged with someone...like Abitibi did with Stone or QUNO did with Donohue and probably the logical merge is with Fletcher Challenge but that's not likely in the cards," Findlay said.
"We (and Fletcher) have divergent directions in mind. So sure we would like to grow (the paper business) and we might even merge it with someone as those companies have.
Asked if Bowater Inc might be interested, Findlay said he did not want to comment.
MacMillan earlier this year turned the paper division into a stand alone business and moved its management to separate offices away from MacMillan's downtown headquarters.
MacMillan has said for more than a year that it was reviewing a range of strategic options for all its operations including acquisitions and divestitures.

In his speech to the annual meeting, Findlay laid out a long-term strategy for the paper business and highlighted the the company's new lightweight coated paper machine in Port Alberni, British Columbia.
"It is a great success story and will serve this company well in the future," he said.
MacMillan's value-added groundwood paper was the most developed in Canada and the paper costs were improving, he said. "This business will provide solid profits in the years ahead," Findlay said.
